nodes.label: Element names and chemical symbols (first 20 elements, Groups 1 & 7, and others in spec)
nodes.objective: Recall and use the names and symbols of the first 20 elements, Group 1 and Group 7 elements, and other specified elements.
essentialPoints: Each element has a unique one- or two-letter chemical symbol (e.g. O, Na)
The first 20 elements plus Groups 1 and 7 and other spec elements must be known by name and symbol

nodes.label: Atoms and elements
nodes.objective: State that all substances are made of atoms and define an atom and an element.
essentialPoints: An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist
An element consists of only one type of atom
There are about 100 different elements, shown in the periodic table

nodes.label: Compounds and chemical reactions
nodes.objective: Define compounds and describe how chemical reactions form new substances.
essentialPoints: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions
Chemical reactions always form one or more new substances, often with a detectable energy change
Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions
Compounds are represented by formulae using element symbols

nodes.label: Writing word and balanced symbol equations
nodes.objective: Write word equations and balanced chemical equations (with state symbols/formulae) for reactions in the specification.
essentialPoints: Word equations show reactants and products by name
Balanced symbol equations use formulae with equal atoms of each element on both sides
Conservation of mass requires balancing

nodes.label: Balanced half equations and ionic equations (HT)
nodes.objective: Write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate (HT only).
essentialPoints: Half equations show electron transfer at an electrode (oxidation or reduction)
Ionic equations show only the species that actually change, omitting spectator ions

nodes.label: Mixtures
nodes.objective: Define a mixture and explain that no chemical reaction is needed to form or separate one.
essentialPoints: A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined
Each substance in a mixture keeps its own chemical properties
Mixtures can be separated by physical processes without new substances being made

nodes.label: Separation technique: filtration
nodes.objective: Describe and explain filtration as a technique for separating an insoluble solid from a liquid.
essentialPoints: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper
Used to obtain residue and filtrate

nodes.label: Separation technique: crystallisation
nodes.objective: Describe and explain crystallisation as a technique for obtaining a solute as solid crystals from a solution.
essentialPoints: A solution is heated to evaporate solvent until saturated, then cooled to form crystals
Used to obtain a soluble salt from its solution

nodes.label: Separation technique: simple distillation
nodes.objective: Describe and explain simple distillation for separating a solvent from a solution.
essentialPoints: Liquid is heated to evaporate the solvent, which is then condensed and collected
Separates a solvent (e.g. water) from dissolved solutes, leaving solute behind

nodes.label: Separation technique: fractional distillation
nodes.objective: Describe and explain fractional distillation for separating a mixture of miscible liquids with different boiling points.
essentialPoints: A fractionating column allows separation of liquids with different boiling points
Vapours condense at different heights/temperatures corresponding to their boiling points

nodes.label: Separation technique: chromatography
nodes.objective: Describe and explain paper chromatography as a technique for separating substances based on differing solubility/affinity for a stationary phase.
essentialPoints: Chromatography separates mixtures based on distribution between a mobile and stationary phase
Different substances travel different distances depending on their attraction to each phase

nodes.label: Selecting an appropriate separation/purification technique
nodes.objective: Suggest a suitable separation or purification technique for a mixture given information about its components.
essentialPoints: Choice of technique depends on properties of the mixture (solubility, boiling point, particle size, colour)
Different techniques suit different combinations of solid/liquid mixtures

nodes.label: Titration technique: using a burette, pipette and indicator to find an end-point
nodes.objective: Carry out an acid-alkali titration accurately using a burette, pipette and indicator to identify the end-point.
essentialPoints: A pipette measures a fixed volume of one solution into a conical flask with indicator
A burette is used to add the second solution dropwise until the indicator changes colour (end-point)
A rough titration followed by accurate concordant titrations improves reliability

nodes.label: Atomic model history: solid sphere and plum pudding models
nodes.objective: Describe the early solid sphere model of the atom and the plum pudding model that followed the discovery of the electron.
essentialPoints: Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny indivisible spheres
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it

nodes.label: Alpha particle scattering experiment and the nuclear model
nodes.objective: Explain how the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment led to replacement of the plum pudding model with the nuclear model.
essentialPoints: Alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil; most passed through but some deflected or bounced back
This showed mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus
This evidence replaced the plum pudding model with the nuclear model

nodes.label: Bohr's model: electrons in fixed energy levels
nodes.objective: Describe Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, proposing electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (energy levels).
essentialPoints: Bohr proposed electrons orbit the nucleus only at specific, fixed distances (energy levels/shells)
Bohr's theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations

nodes.label: Discovery of the proton
nodes.objective: Describe how later experiments showed the nuclear positive charge could be subdivided into protons of equal positive charge.
essentialPoints: Experiments showed the positive charge of the nucleus is made of whole-number units
Each unit of positive charge was named the proton

nodes.label: Chadwick's discovery of the neutron
nodes.objective: State that James Chadwick's experimental work provided evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.
essentialPoints: Chadwick's experimental work provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus
This occurred about 20 years after the nuclear model became accepted

nodes.label: How new evidence changes a scientific model
nodes.objective: Explain that scientific models are changed or replaced when new experimental evidence emerges.
essentialPoints: A scientific model can be changed or replaced when new evidence does not fit the existing model
This is illustrated by the historical development of the atomic model

nodes.label: Relative electrical charges of protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.objective: State the relative charges of protons (+1), neutrons (0) and electrons (-1).
essentialPoints: Protons have a relative charge of +1
Neutrons have a relative charge of 0
Electrons have a relative charge of -1

nodes.label: Atomic number and neutral atoms
nodes.objective: Explain that atoms have no overall charge because protons equal electrons, and define atomic number.
essentialPoints: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons
Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom of an element
All atoms of a given element have the same number of protons; different elements have different numbers of protons

nodes.label: Size and scale of atoms and nuclei
nodes.objective: State the approximate radius of an atom and of a nucleus, and relate these to standard form and everyday scale.
essentialPoints: Atoms have a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10^-10 m)
A nucleus has a radius less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius (about 1 x 10^-14 m)
Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus

nodes.label: Relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons
nodes.objective: State the relative masses of a proton, neutron and electron.
essentialPoints: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1
Electrons have a relative mass that is very small (about 1/1835), often treated as negligible

nodes.label: Mass number
nodes.objective: Define mass number as the sum of protons and neutrons in an atom.
essentialPoints: Mass number = number of protons + number of neutrons

nodes.label: Isotopes
nodes.objective: Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
essentialPoints: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons
Isotopes therefore have different mass numbers

nodes.label: Calculating numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms/ions
nodes.objective: Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion given its atomic number and mass number.
essentialPoints: Number of protons = atomic number
Number of neutrons = mass number - atomic number
Number of electrons = number of protons ± charge for ions

nodes.label: Relative atomic mass from isotopic abundance
nodes.objective: Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the percentage abundances of its isotopes.
essentialPoints: Relative atomic mass is a weighted average accounting for isotope abundance
Calculated as sum of (isotope mass x % abundance) / 100

nodes.label: Electronic structure of atoms (energy levels/shells)
nodes.objective: Represent the electronic structure of the first 20 elements using numbers or diagrams, with electrons filling the lowest available energy levels.
essentialPoints: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (shells) first
Electronic structure can be written as numbers (e.g. 2,8,1 for sodium) or shown as a diagram
Shells fill in order: 2, then 8, then 8 (for the first 20 elements)

nodes.label: Arrangement of the periodic table by atomic number and groups
nodes.objective: Describe how elements are arranged in the periodic table by atomic number into periods and groups of similar properties.
essentialPoints: Elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number
Elements with similar properties are placed in the same column (group)
Similar properties recur at regular intervals, giving the table its 'periodic' name

nodes.label: Groups and outer-shell electrons determine chemical properties
nodes.objective: Explain that elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, giving them similar chemical properties, and relate group/period position to electronic structure and atomic number.
essentialPoints: Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons
This shared outer electron number causes similar chemical properties
Position in the periodic table can be explained by/predicted from electronic structure and atomic number

nodes.label: Predicting reactions and reactivity from periodic table position
nodes.objective: Predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements based on their position in the periodic table.
essentialPoints: Elements' likely reactions and reactivity can be predicted from their group and period position
This relies on the shared outer-electron structure within groups

nodes.label: Early periodic tables based on atomic weight
nodes.objective: Describe how scientists before the discovery of subatomic particles classified elements by atomic weight, and the limitations of this approach.
essentialPoints: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were known, elements were ordered by atomic weight
Early tables were incomplete, and strict atomic-weight order sometimes placed elements in inappropriate groups

nodes.label: Mendeleev's periodic table: gaps and predictions
nodes.objective: Describe how Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and altered atomic-weight order to fit properties, and how later discoveries and isotopes confirmed and refined his table.
essentialPoints: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements he believed were undiscovered
He sometimes reordered elements based on properties rather than strict atomic weight
Elements with Mendeleev's predicted properties were later discovered, filling the gaps
Knowledge of isotopes later explained remaining anomalies in atomic-weight order

nodes.label: Metals and non-metals defined by ion formation
nodes.objective: Define metals and non-metals in terms of their tendency to form positive ions, and locate them on the periodic table.
essentialPoints: Metals are elements that react to form positive ions
Non-metals are elements that do not form positive ions
Metals are found to the left/bottom of the periodic table; non-metals to the right/top

nodes.label: Explaining metal/non-metal properties from atomic structure and position
nodes.objective: Explain the differing physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals in terms of their atomic structure and periodic table position.
essentialPoints: Metal/non-metal physical and chemical properties differ because of differences in atomic structure (outer electrons)
Reactions of elements relate to their electron arrangement and atomic number

nodes.label: Group 0: stable outer shells and lack of reactivity
nodes.objective: Explain why the noble gases are unreactive in terms of their stable outer-shell electron arrangements.
essentialPoints: Group 0 elements (noble gases) are unreactive and rarely form molecules
They have full/stable outer electron shells: 8 electrons, except helium which has 2

nodes.label: Group 0: boiling point trend down the group
nodes.objective: Describe and predict how boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass down the group.
essentialPoints: Boiling points of noble gases increase going down the group
This trend correlates with increasing relative atomic mass

nodes.label: Group 1 reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water
nodes.objective: Describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) with oxygen, chlorine and water.
essentialPoints: Alkali metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides
Alkali metals react with chlorine to form metal chlorides
Alkali metals react with water to form metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas, becoming more vigorous down the group

nodes.label: Group 1: reactivity increases down the group
nodes.objective: Explain why reactivity of Group 1 elements increases going down the group, linked to outer-shell electron arrangement.
essentialPoints: Reactivity of alkali metals increases going down the group
Explained by the single outer electron becoming easier to lose as atomic radius increases and it is further from the nucleus

nodes.label: Group 7: nature of compounds formed with metals and non-metals
nodes.objective: Describe the nature of compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
essentialPoints: Halogens are non-metals existing as diatomic molecules (pairs of atoms)
Reaction of a halogen with a metal produces an ionic salt (metal halide)
Reaction of a halogen with a non-metal produces a molecular (covalent) compound

nodes.label: Group 7: trends in relative molecular mass, melting and boiling point
nodes.objective: Describe how relative molecular mass, melting point and boiling point increase down Group 7.
essentialPoints: Further down Group 7, relative molecular mass increases
Melting point and boiling point both increase down the group

nodes.label: Group 7: reactivity decreases down the group
nodes.objective: Explain why reactivity of Group 7 elements decreases going down the group, linked to outer-shell electron arrangement.
essentialPoints: Reactivity of halogens decreases going down the group
Explained by increasing atomic radius making it harder to attract/gain an extra electron into the outer shell

nodes.label: Halogen displacement reactions
nodes.objective: Describe and explain how a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its salt.
essentialPoints: A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt
This demonstrates the reactivity trend down Group 7
Displacement is evidenced by a colour change in solution

nodes.label: Predicting group properties from electron arrangement and trends
nodes.objective: Predict properties of Group 0, 1 and 7 elements from given trends down each group, based on outer-shell electron arrangement.
essentialPoints: Properties of Group 0, 1 and 7 elements can be predicted from established trends down the group
Predictions are grounded in the shared outer-shell electron count within each group

nodes.label: Transition metals compared with Group 1 elements
nodes.objective: Describe how transition metals differ from Group 1 metals in melting point, density, strength, hardness and reactivity, exemplified by Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
essentialPoints: Transition metals have higher melting points, densities, strength and hardness than Group 1 metals
Transition metals are much less reactive with oxygen, water and halogens than Group 1 metals
Examples: Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu

nodes.label: Typical properties of transition metals: variable ions, coloured compounds, catalysts
nodes.objective: Describe the typical properties of transition elements: forming ions with different charges, forming coloured compounds, and acting as catalysts, exemplified by Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
essentialPoints: Many transition elements form ions with different charges (variable oxidation states)
Transition element compounds are often coloured
Transition elements and their compounds are often useful as catalysts
